title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Patient—It's the Caregiver Who Gets Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patient's condition itself, but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses, forces a post-90s worker to quit, love is the starting point but not the support, and the system hasn't caught up with these families.
why: This isn't elderly wellness science; it's a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families—no standard answers, only realities you need to see before it's too late.
who: Only children born in the 1980s and 1990s, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they've made no elder-care plans; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care gap eventually falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the population; 35 million are disabled elderly, yet there are only about 500,000 care workers. The supply gap isn't absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patients account for nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies mislead
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia comes mostly from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the professor's incontinence in Still Alice is just one form. He met an elderly man who, despite dementia from his tailor background, would still notice stains on visitors' clothes and teach them to remove them with orange peel; and another who, after a car accident left him disabled, could only hum Liuyang River with focused expression. Dementia covers multiple causes—Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, etc.—and each person's life imprint lingers differently; care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on state nursing insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents shop and go to cafés like ordinary people, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose how hard it is to replicate: the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over €18 million, of which €17.8 million came from the government, and residents' fees are also covered by long-term care–related schemes. In contrast, Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home that elevators had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice drags down caregivers
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between "I love my parents very much" and "I'm about to be dragged down by them." Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse must learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers become patients too.

points.h: The more you see, the less prepared you feel for old age
points.body: Having studied elder care for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child; both parents are 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less confident he feels. His research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange care for her own parents. Multi-child families also have friction: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved parents to Shenzhen found rent, medical costs, and nanny fees rising faster than retirement wages. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who could initially paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later could only praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another woman's husband reported new losses weekly: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long haul of care isn't repetitive hardship; it's facing a small goodbye every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived but doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, expanded to about 90 cities by around 2025, with the official pace aiming for universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that it's not cash for every senior; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and similar services—mild cases may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and seniors, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair would fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the share choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear on its own.

terms.def: A Dutch dementia village: a closed community for people with severe dementia where staff pose as residents to maintain a normal living atmosphere.
A book by Arthur Kleinman proposing that care is not one-way help but a relationship.
Unpaid care provided by spouses, children, and other family members, as opposed to paid caregivers.
A social insurance that pays for care services for disabled or demented elderly, not a cash subsidy.

"It's like riding a slide—you're going downhill. So at that moment, I think this kind of care is indeed long and drawn-out."
"I think love is a very important foundation, but it shouldn't be the only condition for care. It still needs external resources, including social support, and so on."
